## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No results yet, and scores stay hidden, so later rounds won't tell us which candidates work. The best plan is a few well-reasoned, varied bets that are unlikely to crash. Two things about the task matter here. First, the default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples each, so the recipe may count for as much as the architecture. Second, whether a brick is correct depends on its landing layer: the highest filled cell under its footprint must match the target at that layer, and the brick must not seal missing target cells below it. The starting network flattens the layers into channels and has to work this out implicitly. A shared per-layer scoring head, with scores combined over layers, builds this structure in. I keep it cheap (about 1.05x the starting compute) so it keeps nearly the full sample budget. Candidates: the starting network with a tuned recipe, the per-layer head with the default recipe, and the per-layer head with the tuned recipe.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors, but no scores are shown, so I can't rank them. Selection is blind, so the best plan is a spread of candidates that are each likely to be strong, not careful one-change ablations. From the task structure, two things probably matter most. First, sample efficiency: the default recipe gets only about 32 PPO updates. Fewer epochs and smaller batches give more samples and many more updates. Second, precise per-cell matching inside each brick footprint: the starting head only sees max, min and mean of features blurred by 3x3 convolutions, which may not be enough to check that each cell matches the target at the landing layer. This round tests: (1) the starting network with a fast-update recipe (2 epochs, about 237 updates); (2) a head that runs a learned convolution over each brick footprint, with a skip connection from the stem; (3) the per-layer head from round 1 with the fast recipe.

### Round 3
No scores are visible. All six trials trained without errors. That includes the fast recipe (64–128 envs, 2 epochs, about 230–240k steps), so the time limit has not been a problem at roughly 1x compute. Because only seed noise and priors are available, the plan is to keep the comparisons clean. A1 isolates the head: it pairs the footprint-convolution head from r2c2 with r2c1's exact recipe. A2 isolates the recipe: it keeps the baseline network and pushes the samples-versus-reuse trade further, to 1 PPO epoch and about 400k steps. A3 tests something not yet tried, global context. One self-attention block on the conv trunk could help with ordering and the DONE decision, because those depend on the whole design, not on a 5x5 neighbourhood. I avoided 3D convolutions and big compute increases because of the time limit and the sample cost. Each candidate stays at or below about 1.5x the starting compute.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so the trials can't be ranked. All nine trained without errors, and the two-seed noise is unknown. The search covered three families of ideas: recipes with more frequent updates (fewer envs, 1–3 epochs, gamma 0.97, lambda 0.95), placement heads that model the brick (learned footprint convolution, per-layer logsumexp head), and global attention. This is the last round, so each proposal combines parts that already train cleanly into a plausible best candidate. One gives the footprint-conv head the 1-epoch, ~400k-sample recipe (r3c2's recipe). One adds a cheap dilated residual conv to the footprint-conv model, which widens the receptive field without the cost of attention. One gives the per-layer head the 1-epoch recipe. All stay near 1–1.4x compute so they finish well inside the time limit. No result will tell me which recipe was better, because the scores are hidden, but the final selection uses the real dev scores.
